stem: According to the chapter, what does the word symmetry refer to?
options: Parts of a figure that repeat in a definite pattern
Parts of a figure that are drawn in bright colours
A figure that is drawn using only straight line segments
A figure whose parts are all of different sizes
explanation: Correct option: (A). The chapter says a symmetry refers to a part or parts of a figure that are repeated in some definite pattern. Bright colours make a picture attractive but do not make it symmetrical; symmetrical figures such as a flower can have curved boundaries; and parts of different sizes do not repeat.

Butterfly
Pinwheel

stem: In the rangoli, the red petals come back onto themselves when the rangoli is rotated by 90 degrees about its centre. Through which other turn will the red petals also come back onto themselves?
options: 45 degrees
180 degrees
60 degrees
120 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (B). A turn of 180 degrees is two turns of 90 degrees one after the other. Since each 90 degree turn brings the petals back onto themselves, doing it twice does too. A 45 degree turn is only half of the smallest turn known to work, and 60 and 120 degrees are not made up of 90 degree turns, so there is no reason for the petals to fit after them.

stem: Mira says the butterfly picture is symmetrical. Which reason best supports her claim?
options: Its wings are much bigger than its thin, light body
Its wings are coloured in very bright shades
It can fly about freely in many directions
Its left half is a mirror image of its right half
explanation: Correct option: (D). Symmetry is about parts repeating in a definite pattern; for the butterfly, one half repeats the other as a mirror image, so the middle line is a line of symmetry. The size of the wings, their colours and how a butterfly flies do not show any repeating pattern in the picture.

stem: The pinwheel at the start of the chapter has no line of symmetry, yet the chapter calls it symmetrical. Which statement explains this best?
options: Its two halves overlap when it is folded in half
Every figure with a hexagon in it is symmetrical
Its parts repeat when it is turned about its centre
Its parts are all different in shape from one another
explanation: Correct option: (C). A figure can be symmetrical without a line of symmetry: the pinwheel's parts repeat in a definite pattern as you move around (turn about) the centre of the hexagon. Folding does not give overlapping halves because it has no line of symmetry; having a hexagon inside does not by itself make a figure symmetrical; and parts that are all different would mean no repetition at all.

stem: Which of these describes a line of symmetry of a figure?
options: It cuts the figure into two parts of equal area, whatever their shape
It cuts the figure into two parts that overlap exactly on folding
It joins any two opposite corners of the given figure
It passes through the centre point of any given figure
explanation: Correct option: (B). A line of symmetry cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when the figure is folded along that line (mirror halves). Equal area is not enough: the two parts must also match in shape. A line joining opposite corners works for a square but not for a rectangle that is not a square, and not every line through the centre is a line of symmetry.

stem: By folding a square piece of paper, how many lines of symmetry can you find?
explanation: Correct option: (D). A square can be folded into overlapping halves in four ways: vertically, horizontally and along each of its two diagonals, so it has 4 lines of symmetry. 1 or 2 counts only some of the folds, and there is no other way to fold it, so 8 is too many.

stem: A rectangular sheet that is not a square is folded along one of its diagonals. What do you observe?
options: The parts overlap exactly, so the diagonal is a line of symmetry
The parts overlap only when the rectangle is very long and thin
The parts do not overlap, so the diagonal is not a line of symmetry
The parts have unequal areas, so the fold is not a line of symmetry
explanation: Correct option: (C). When a rectangle that is not a square is folded along a diagonal, the corners of one half stick out beyond the other half, so the parts do not overlap; the diagonal is not a line of symmetry (unlike for a square). A long, thin rectangle fails even more clearly. The two triangles do have equal areas; they fail because they do not fit on top of each other after folding.

stem: Which triangle has exactly three lines of symmetry?
options: A triangle with all three sides equal
A triangle with exactly two sides equal
A triangle with all three sides different
A triangle with a right angle and unequal sides
explanation: Correct option: (A). A triangle with equal sides and equal angles can be folded onto itself along the line from each corner to the middle of the opposite side, giving 3 lines of symmetry. A triangle with exactly two equal sides has only 1 line of symmetry, and a triangle with all sides different (including a right triangle with unequal sides) has none.

stem: Can a triangle have exactly two lines of symmetry?
options: Yes; a right triangle with two equal sides has exactly two lines
Yes; a triangle with two equal sides and one longer side
No; two such lines would make all sides equal, giving three
No; a triangle can never have even one line of symmetry
explanation: Correct option: (C). Each line of symmetry of a triangle passes through a corner and makes the two sides at that corner equal. Two different lines would make two different pairs of sides equal, so all three sides would be equal, and such a triangle has three lines of symmetry, not two. A right triangle with two equal sides, or any triangle with exactly two equal sides, has only one line of symmetry; and many triangles do have lines of symmetry.

stem: A figure that has one or more lines of symmetry is also said to have which kind of symmetry?
options: Rotational symmetry
Point symmetry
No symmetry at all
Reflection symmetry
explanation: Correct option: (D). The chapter says a figure that has a line or lines of symmetry is also said to have reflection symmetry, because each side is reflected by the line onto the other side. Rotational symmetry is about turning, not folding, and a figure may have a line of symmetry without it. Point symmetry is not the term used here, and such a figure is certainly symmetrical.

stem: What happens when a figure is reflected in one of its lines of symmetry?
options: The figure turns about its centre through a quarter of a turn
Each side moves across the line and the figure looks unchanged
Only the left side moves across; the right side stays in place
The figure becomes twice as large on the other side of the line
explanation: Correct option: (B). Reflecting in a line of symmetry sends the part on one side to the other side and the part on the other side to the first side, so the figure occupies the same place and looks unchanged. A quarter turn is a rotation, not a reflection. Both sides are reflected, not just one, and reflection does not change the size of a figure.

stem: Square ABCD has A at the top left, B at the top right, C at the bottom right and D at the bottom left. It is reflected in its vertical line of symmetry. Where does corner A go?
options: To the position of B
To the position of D
To the position of C
It stays where it is
explanation: Correct option: (A). The vertical line of symmetry runs down the middle, between A and B and between D and C. Reflection sends A on the left to the matching place on the right, which is B's position (and D goes to C's position). D is below A, which would need a horizontal line; C's position is diagonally opposite; and only points on the line itself stay where they are.

stem: Square ABCD has A at the top left, B at the top right, C at the bottom right and D at the bottom left. It is reflected in the diagonal from A to C. What happens to the corners?
options: A and C swap places; B and D stay in place
A goes to B's place; C goes to D's place
A and C stay in place; B and D swap places
All four corners stay in their own places
explanation: Correct option: (C). Points on the line of reflection do not move, so A and C, which lie on the diagonal AC, stay where they are. B and D are on opposite sides of this diagonal at the same distance from it, so they swap places. A and C would swap only under a reflection in the other diagonal BD; 'A goes to B's place' describes the vertical line; and B and D do not lie on AC, so not all corners stay.

stem: Square ABCD has A at the top left, B at the top right, C at the bottom right and D at the bottom left. It is first reflected in its horizontal line of symmetry and then in its vertical line of symmetry. Where does corner A end up?
options: At A's original position
At B's original position
At D's original position
At C's original position
explanation: Correct option: (D). Reflecting in the horizontal line sends A (top left) to the bottom left, D's original position. Reflecting that result in the vertical line sends the bottom left to the bottom right, which is C's original position. A would return to its own place only if it were reflected twice in the same line; B's position comes from the vertical reflection alone, and D's from the horizontal reflection alone.

stem: A paper is folded in half, ink is dropped on one half, and the halves are pressed together and opened. Where is the line of symmetry of the ink blot design?
options: Along an edge of the paper
Along the fold of the paper
Through the biggest drop of ink
The design has no such line
explanation: Correct option: (B). Pressing the halves together copies the ink on one half onto the other half as a mirror image across the fold, so the fold is the line of symmetry. The edges of the paper and the position of the biggest drop do not divide the design into mirror halves, and the design is symmetric, so it does have a line of symmetry.

stem: A square sheet is folded in half vertically and then in half horizontally. A single hole is punched through all the layers. How many holes appear when the sheet is opened out?
explanation: Correct option: (D). The first fold makes 2 layers and the second fold doubles this to 4 layers, so one punch makes 4 holes, one in each quarter, with both fold lines as lines of symmetry. 2 holes would come from one fold only; 3 cannot come from 4 layers; and 8 holes would need a third fold.

stem: A square sheet is folded along its vertical middle line. A hole is punched 2 cm to the left of the fold and 3 cm below the top edge. Where is the other hole when the sheet is unfolded?
options: 2 cm left of the fold, 3 cm above the bottom edge
4 cm right of the fold, 3 cm below the top edge
2 cm right of the fold, 3 cm below the top edge
2 cm right of the fold, 3 cm above the bottom edge
explanation: Correct option: (C). The fold is the line of symmetry, so the second hole is the mirror image of the first across the fold: the same distance (2 cm) from the fold on the other side, and at the same height (3 cm below the top). It is not on the same side of the fold, not twice as far from it, and a vertical fold does not move a hole up or down.

stem: A square sheet is folded in half and in half again, so the centre of the sheet is the closed corner. One straight cut across this corner removes a small triangle whose two sides along the folds are equal. What hole is seen when the sheet is opened?
options: A square, with its corners on the fold lines
A rhombus that is not a square, with corners on the folds
A single right-angled triangle at the centre
Two separate right-angled triangles on the folds
explanation: Correct option: (A). The cut-off triangle has a right angle at the centre and equal sides along the two folds. Unfolding repeats it in all four quarters, giving four such triangles meeting at the centre; together they make one hole with four equal sides and four right angles, a square tilted so its corners lie on the fold lines. A rhombus that is not a square would come from unequal sides along the folds; a single triangle ignores the other layers; and the four pieces meet at the centre as one hole, not two separate triangles.

source.ref: Original practice question (CBSE pattern); NCERT Ganita Prakash, Class 6, Chapter 9 'Symmetry'

stem: What is the fixed point about which a figure is rotated called?
options: The line of symmetry
The angle of symmetry
The centre of rotation
The point of reflection
explanation: Correct option: (C). When talking of rotational symmetry, there is always a fixed point about which the object is rotated, and it is called the centre of rotation. A line of symmetry is a fold line, not a point; an angle of symmetry is how far the figure is turned; and 'point of reflection' is not the term used for turning.

stem: Which of these is an angle of symmetry of every figure?
options: 90 degrees
180 degrees
270 degrees
360 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (D). When any figure is rotated by 360 degrees (a full turn), it comes back to its original position, so 360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry. 90, 180 and 270 degrees work for some figures, such as a square, but not for every figure, for example a scalene triangle.

stem: A square is rotated about its centre. Which list gives all its angles of symmetry?
options: 90 and 360 degrees only
90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees
180 and 360 degrees only
explanation: Correct option: (B). A quarter turn of 90 degrees takes A to B, B to C, C to D and D to A, so the square fits on itself. Repeating this gives 180, 270 and 360 degrees as well, so there are four angles of symmetry. '90 and 360 only' misses the half and three-quarter turns; 45 degrees is not an angle of symmetry, since after a 45 degree turn the corners point to where the middles of the sides were; and '180 and 360 only' is the answer for a rectangle that is not a square.

stem: The paper windmill in the chapter looks the same when rotated by 90 degrees about its centre, but its halves do not overlap when it is folded. Which statement is correct?
options: It has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry
It has a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry
It has both a line of symmetry and rotational symmetry
It has neither a line of symmetry nor rotational symmetry
explanation: Correct option: (A). Since its halves do not overlap on folding, the windmill has no line of symmetry. Since it looks exactly the same after a 90 degree turn, an angle between 0 and 360 degrees, it has rotational symmetry (angles 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees). The other options each get at least one of these two facts wrong.

stem: A strip-shaped figure comes back to its original look only after a complete turn of 360 degrees. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It has rotational symmetry, as 360 degrees is its angle of symmetry
It has no rotational symmetry, as no angle below 360 degrees works
It has rotational symmetry, but only about one of its corners
It has no angle of symmetry at all, not even 360 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (B). A figure has rotational symmetry only when it has an angle of symmetry strictly between 0 and 360 degrees. Every figure has 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry, so that alone does not count; this strip has no smaller angle, so it has no rotational symmetry. Turning it about a corner does not help, and 360 degrees is still an angle of symmetry, so it is wrong to say it has none.

stem: A figure has 3 identical radial arms. What angle between adjacent arms gives it rotational symmetry?
options: 90 degrees
60 degrees
180 degrees
120 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (D). For the rotated figure to overlap the original, the three angles between the arms must all be equal. A full turn of 360 degrees is shared equally, so each angle is 360 / 3 = 120 degrees. 90 degrees suits 4 arms, 60 degrees suits 6 arms, and three angles of 180 degrees would add up to 540 degrees, more than a full turn.

stem: If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number of degrees, what must be true of it?
options: It is a factor of 360
It is a multiple of 360
It is always more than 90
It is an odd number
explanation: Correct option: (A). All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest one, and 360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry, so 360 is a multiple of the smallest angle; that is, the smallest angle is a factor of 360. It cannot be a multiple of 360 unless it is 360 itself; it can be small, such as 60 degrees for 6 arms; and it is often even, such as 90 or 120.

stem: A figure made of equally spaced identical radial arms has exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
options: 51 1/7 degrees
52 4/7 degrees
51 3/7 degrees
50 5/7 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (C). The smallest angle is 360 / 7 degrees. 7 x 51 = 357, leaving a remainder of 3, so 360 / 7 = 51 3/7 degrees, which is not a whole number. 51 1/7 and 50 5/7 come from wrong remainders, and 52 4/7 degrees would give 7 x 52 4/7 = 368 degrees, more than a full turn.

stem: In a figure, 60 degrees is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are its other angles of symmetry?
options: 120, 180 and 240 degrees only
90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees
120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees only
explanation: Correct option: (B). Every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one, up to 360 degrees: 2 x 60 = 120, 3 x 60 = 180, 4 x 60 = 240, 5 x 60 = 300 and 6 x 60 = 360. '120, 180 and 240 only' stops too early, and '120, 180, 240 and 300 only' leaves out 360, which is always an angle of symmetry; 90, 180, 270 and 360 are the angles for a smallest angle of 90, and 90 is not a multiple of 60.

stem: In a figure, 60 degrees is an angle of symmetry, and the figure has exactly two angles of symmetry less than 60 degrees. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
options: 30 degrees
15 degrees
20 degrees
40 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (C). Angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle s, so 60 is a multiple of s. If exactly two angles are below 60, they are s and 2s, and the next one, 3s, is 60. So s = 60 / 3 = 20 degrees (angles 20, 40, 60, ...). With 30 degrees only one angle (30) is below 60; with 15 degrees there are three (15, 30, 45); and 40 degrees cannot be the smallest because 60 is not a multiple of 40.

Only 180 and 360 degrees

stem: Which figure has a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry?
options: A triangle with all three of its sides equal
A hexagon with equal sides and angles
A triangle with exactly two equal sides
A rectangle that is not a square
explanation: Correct option: (C). stem: Read the case 'The Ashoka Chakra'. What will Kavya and Farhan find about the number of lines of symmetry and the smallest angle of symmetry?
options: 12 lines of symmetry; smallest angle 30 degrees
24 lines of symmetry; smallest angle 24 degrees
48 lines of symmetry; smallest angle 7.5 degrees
24 lines of symmetry; smallest angle 15 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (D). With 24 identical, equally spaced spokes, the wheel fits on itself after turning from one spoke to the next: 360 / 24 = 15 degrees, so the smallest angle of symmetry is 15 degrees and there are 24 angles of symmetry. Kavya finds 24 fold lines: the 24 spokes lie on 12 lines through the centre, and the 12 lines midway between neighbouring spokes are also lines of symmetry. 12 lines counts only the spoke lines, 24 degrees confuses the number of spokes with the angle, and 48 lines with 7.5 degrees would need 48 spokes.
